title: Interpreting Prediction Market Prices as Probabilities
status: NBER Working Paper 12200; this cited version is not a peer-reviewed journal article
verification: NBER HTML citation metadata and complete landing-page abstract inspected; paper full text not inspected.
supports: The paper gives sufficient conditions linking prices to mean beliefs and discusses useful but sometimes biased approximations outside those conditions.
Risk aversion and the distribution of beliefs matter to interpretation.
limitations: Mean belief is not objective truth or demonstrated calibration.
Does not establish that an arbitrary stale, thin, or constrained market price equals event probability.
locator: NBER abstract immediately following Issue Date

title: Interpreting the Predictions of Prediction Markets
status: NBER Working Paper 10359; cited as the working paper, not a later journal version
verification: NBER HTML citation metadata and complete landing-page abstract inspected; full text not inspected.
supports: Under the specified risk-neutral, price-taking model with heterogeneous beliefs, equilibrium price only partially identifies central tendency and does not identify belief dispersion.
limitations: A model-dependent identification argument, not a claim that market prices contain no information.
Do not attach an unverified later journal DOI to this entry.

title: Prediction Markets
status: Published scholarly synthesis with empirical comparisons; Journal of Economic Perspectives 18(2), 107-126
verification: AEA publisher citation metadata and abstract inspected.
supports: The paper assembles evidence on information aggregation and predictive accuracy across multiple prediction-market contexts.
Conditional market interpretations do not automatically distinguish correlation from causation.
limitations: A synthesis and selected empirical contexts, not a contemporary venue-wide performance estimate.
Forecast accuracy does not demonstrate trading profit after costs.

title: Prediction market accuracy in the long run
status: Peer-reviewed; International Journal of Forecasting 24(2), 285-300 according to publisher-deposited DOI metadata
verification: University of Iowa IEM author-institution abstract inspected; DOI identity, authors, year, volume and pages cross-checked in publisher-deposited Crossref record. Direct publisher page was inaccessible.
supports: The abstract compares contemporaneous IEM vote-share forecasts with 964 national polls across five U.S. presidential elections from 1988 through 2004.
It reports the market closer to the eventual two-major-party vote split in 74 percent of those comparisons.
limitations: 964 polls are not 964 independent elections.
Vote-share forecasting is not the same estimand as a winner-take-all probability.
The IEM page lists 283-298 while the DOI record lists 285-300; the bibliographic discrepancy is disclosed rather than silently treated as resolved.
No post-cost profitability inference.

title: Logarithmic Market Scoring Rules for Modular Combinatorial Information Aggregation
status: Journal article; The Journal of Prediction Markets 1(1), 3-15
verification: Publisher abstract and HTML citation metadata inspected. Citation date and issue identify 2007; later web-deposit dates are not publication dates. Indexed title contains the typo 'MARKETS CORING'; this entry normalizes it to 'Market Scoring'.
supports: Market scoring rules combine individual elicitation with group information aggregation.
The abstract describes special conditional-probability preservation properties of logarithmic rules.
limitations: Full theorem and cost-function derivations were not inspected in this audit; derive classroom identities explicitly.
An LMSR teaching mechanism is not a description of every live exchange.
locator: Publisher abstract; citation_volume, citation_issue, citation_date metadata

title: Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation
status: Peer-reviewed review and methods article; Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(477), 359-378
verification: Author-hosted University of Washington article inspected in memory: abstract and Section 1 (p. 359), Section 2.1 definitions (p. 360), Section 2.3 (p. 362), and Sections 3.1-3.2 (pp. 362-364), including Theorem 2, Examples 1 and 3, and the binary representation. Not all 20 pages or proofs inspected. Printed metadata confirms the DOI, journal, date and authors.
supports: Proper scores reward reporting the generating distribution in expectation; strict propriety makes the maximizer unique, relative to the stated forecast class.
Categorical quadratic/Brier and logarithmic scores are strictly proper, with the paper using a higher-is-better reward orientation.
Direct forecast-score comparisons require the same set of forecast situations; differing intrinsic predictability can confound comparisons.
The categorical squared-error sum includes both binary outcomes and therefore is twice the book's single-YES loss after reversing the reward sign.
limitations: Strict propriety is an expectation-level property, not a guarantee of finite-sample calibration or profitable decisions after execution costs.
The paper's reward orientation must be reversed for the book's loss convention; zero probability assigned to an occurring outcome can give infinite log loss.
Do not assume an outcome-dependent normalized skill score remains proper merely because its underlying score is proper.
locator: Sections 1, 2.1, 2.3 and 3.1-3.2; pp. 359-360 and 362-364; categorical Examples 1 and 3

title: Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability
status: Published journal article; Monthly Weather Review 78(1), 1-3
verification: Publisher-deposited Crossref identity, title, author, date and pagination inspected. Follow-up AMS landing-page and public PDF-interface attempts returned 403; the legacy NOAA library archive hostname did not resolve. Original text remains uninspected. The independently inspected GNEITING2007 Section 3.1 explicitly presents the categorical Brier score, but is not represented as an inspection of this original article.
supports: Verified bibliographic pointer to Brier's probability-forecast verification paper.
limitations: Do not claim the original paper uses precisely the book's single-YES binary normalization without inspecting the original.
The book must define its own scoring convention explicitly; use the inspected GNEITING2007 Examples 1 and 3 for substantive scoring support.
locator: Crossref DOI metadata; original-text follow-up required

title: A New Vector Partition of the Probability Score
status: Published journal article; Journal of Applied Meteorology 12(4), 595-600
verification: Publisher-deposited DOI metadata inspected. Follow-up AMS abstract and public PDF endpoints remained inaccessible with 403 responses; no lawful accessible original manuscript was established. Original abstract/full text remains uninspected.
supports: Bibliographic reading pointer for probability-score decomposition.
limitations: This metadata-only record does not verify a particular sample decomposition or binned calibration identity.
Distinguish population identities from estimates constructed with arbitrary bins.

title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
status: Peer-reviewed ICML proceedings; PMLR 70, 1321-1330
verification: Primary proceedings abstract and bibliographic export inspected.
supports: Modern neural networks in the studied image/document classification experiments can be poorly calibrated.
Temperature scaling was effective on most datasets considered by the authors.
limitations: Not an assurance of calibration on prediction markets or under distribution shift.
No guarantee that a small calibration sample can safely fit a flexible map.

title: Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning
status: Peer-reviewed ICML 2005 proceedings, 625-632
verification: Cornell author manuscript inspected in memory: abstract and introduction opening (PDF p. 1), Platt scaling and isotonic regression methods and dataset description (p. 2), qualitative experimental setup/discussion (p. 3), and Figure 8 discussion plus Section 7 conclusions (p. 8). Not every intermediate experiment or figure inspected.
supports: Training a calibration map on the same examples used to fit the base model can introduce bias; the paper uses independent calibration samples.
Platt scaling fits a sigmoid; isotonic regression fits a monotone map and can overfit when calibration data are small.
The paper's eight binary-classification problems exhibit model-dependent probability distortions and calibration benefits; calibration can also hurt already well-calibrated models.
limitations: The original experiments use random samples, not event-grouped chronological evaluation; that design cannot be transplanted unchanged into historical market research.
The original comparison reuses calibration data for model selection and reserves a final test set; it does not authorize tuning on the final evaluation set.
The 2005 neural-network findings and the modern networks in GUO2017 concern different architectures/data; neither is a universal ranking.
locator: Author PDF pp. 1-3 and 8; Sections 2.1-2.2, 3-4 and 7; Figure 8 discussion

title: Beta calibration: a well-founded and easily implemented improvement on logistic calibration for binary classifiers
status: Peer-reviewed AISTATS proceedings; PMLR 54, 623-631
verification: Primary proceedings abstract and bibliographic export inspected.
supports: The abstract explains that isotonic calibration can overfit small datasets and that logistic calibration can worsen certain already calibrated or skewed scores.
The paper proposes a richer beta-calibration family.
limitations: Its comparative results concern studied classifiers and datasets, especially Naive Bayes and AdaBoost.
No calibration method is universally beneficial on future event markets.

title: Regularization Paths for Generalized Linear Models via Coordinate Descent
status: Peer-reviewed; Journal of Statistical Software 33(1), 1-22
verification: Publisher HTML citation metadata, citation export, and abstract inspected.
supports: Coordinate-descent regularization paths cover linear, binary logistic, and multinomial models with lasso, ridge, and elastic-net penalties.
The methods can exploit sparse features.
limitations: Computational scalability is not evidence of out-of-sample event forecasting advantage.
Scaling, penalty selection and validation remain analysis decisions.

title: Regression Shrinkage and Selection Via the Lasso
status: Peer-reviewed; Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 58(1), 267-288
verification: Publisher-deposited Crossref metadata and deposited abstract excerpt inspected; no direct full text inspected.
supports: The proposed least-squares method constrains the sum of absolute coefficient values and can produce exactly zero coefficients.
limitations: The abstract's primary setup is linear regression; generalized-model implementation is separately supported by FRIEDMAN2010.
Sparse selection is not proof of causal importance.

title: A weakly informative default prior distribution for logistic and other regression models
status: Peer-reviewed; The Annals of Applied Statistics 2(4); author manuscript deposited on arXiv in 2009
verification: Author-deposited arXiv abstract and metadata inspected; journal year/volume cross-checked against publisher-deposited Crossref metadata.
supports: The paper proposes scaled predictors and weakly informative Student-t priors for logistic regression.
The abstract discusses obtaining estimates under complete separation.
limitations: A proposed default is not a universal best prior.
Prior scale and predictor scaling are part of the model; Bayesian intervals do not remove misspecification.

title: Random Forests
status: Peer-reviewed; Machine Learning 45(1), 5-32
verification: Publisher-deposited DOI metadata inspected. Relevant author-maintained Berkeley explanatory text was read at https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/RandomForests/cc_home.htm (Introduction, Overview and tree-construction description); original journal full text not inspected.
supports: The inspected author description builds classification trees using bootstrap samples and random feature subsets at splits, then aggregates their votes.
limitations: The explanatory website is not the journal article's full proof.
Tree votes need not be calibrated probabilities; event dependence limits naive out-of-bag interpretation.
locator: Berkeley author site, Overview and tree-construction description

title: Greedy function approximation: A gradient boosting machine
status: Peer-reviewed; The Annals of Statistics 29(5)
verification: Publisher-deposited DOI metadata inspected. Follow-up Project Euclid landing/download routes returned failure/non-article content. The historical Stanford hostname failed DNS and the current jerryfriedman.su.domains manuscript route had an expired TLS certificate; validation was not disabled. Original abstract/full text remains uninspected.
supports: Bibliographic reading pointer for the gradient-boosting-machine formulation.
limitations: Metadata does not verify a specific algorithm, theorem, or empirical claim; inspect relevant text before detailed attribution.
Do not equate training-loss improvement with held-out calibration.

title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System
status: Peer-reviewed KDD 2016 paper; arXiv author version identifies KDD publication
verification: arXiv author-deposited abstract, authors, version history, KDD note and related publisher DOI inspected.
supports: The paper introduces a scalable boosting system with sparsity-aware processing and weighted quantile sketches.
limitations: Scale and benchmark performance do not show event-market profitability.
No requirement that this book depend on the XGBoost package or reproduce its full system.

title: Regression Models and Life-Tables
status: Peer-reviewed; Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 34(2), 187-202
verification: Publisher-deposited DOI metadata and abstract inspected; direct publisher page was inaccessible.
supports: The paper treats censored failure times with covariate effects multiplying an unspecified baseline hazard.
limitations: Outcome occurrence and contractual settlement are different times.
A proportional-hazard model requires justified assumptions; arbitrary binary contracts are not automatically survival problems.

title: A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems
status: Published journal article; Journal of Basic Engineering 82(1), 35-45
verification: Publisher-deposited Crossref metadata and abstract inspected; original full text not inspected.
supports: The abstract describes a state-transition formulation of linear filtering with recursive error-covariance calculations.
limitations: It is a linear filtering foundation, not a ready-made model of bounded binary contract prices.
Do not silently assume Gaussian observation noise for binary outcomes.

title: Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection
status: arXiv:0710.3742; no peer-reviewed journal version established in this audit
verification: Author-deposited arXiv abstract, authors and version date inspected.
supports: The paper derives online inference for the current run length under its changepoint model.
limitations: The abstract assumes parameters before and after a changepoint are independent.
A detected change is not proof of a causal regime shift or a trading opportunity.

title: Introduction to Information Retrieval
status: Cambridge University Press textbook; author-hosted online edition
verification: Author-site bibliographic page inspected. Relevant HTML text read: Term frequency and weighting; Inverse document frequency; initial Naive Bayes text classification section through parameter estimation and zero-count discussion. Not the whole book.
supports: Bag-of-words representations discard word order.
Inverse document frequency uses document-level occurrence frequency.
Multinomial Naive Bayes combines class priors with term likelihoods and can compute in log space to avoid underflow.
limitations: Text representation and classification foundations do not establish financial predictive value.
Vocabulary and document-frequency estimation must use the appropriate training corpus; historical language-model contamination is a separate issue.

title: Learning representations by back-propagating errors
status: Peer-reviewed; Nature 323(6088), 533-536
verification: Hinton's University of Toronto scanned article visually inspected on pp. 533-535 (PDF pp. 1-3): title/abstract, feed-forward model, squared-error objective, chain-rule equations 1-9, illustrative representations and local-minimum discussion. The final page was not inspected. Images were rendered only for inspection and removed afterward.
supports: Back-propagation computes weight derivatives by propagating output-error derivatives backward through differentiable layers.
The inspected derivation uses a squared-error objective and gives gradient and momentum updates.
The paper explicitly notes that local minima prevent a guarantee of finding a global minimum.
limitations: These demonstrations do not establish calibrated probabilities or predictive value on markets.
Do not assert exclusive historical priority; the inspected paper itself acknowledges independently discovered variants.
A gradient calculation is not a guarantee of successful representation learning from a small dependent event sample.
locator: Nature pp. 533-535; equations 1-9 and local-minimum discussion

title: Long Short-Term Memory
status: Peer-reviewed; Neural Computation 9(8), 1735-1780
verification: Publisher-deposited DOI metadata and abstract inspected; no original full-text inspection.
supports: The abstract introduces LSTM to address decaying error signals in learning long dependencies.
Reported experiments in the abstract include artificial sequence data.
limitations: Artificial long-delay tasks are not evidence that an LSTM will outperform simple probability models on sparse event data.
Do not equate a sequence of quote updates with many independent outcomes.

title: Attention Is All You Need
status: NeurIPS 2017 paper; inspected author repository version is arXiv:1706.03762v7, dated 2023
verification: arXiv abstract, author list and version history inspected; relevant full HTML Section 4, Why Self-Attention, inspected at https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7. Not all training/results sections inspected.
supports: The Transformer replaces recurrence/convolution with attention in the proposed sequence-transduction architecture.
Section 4 compares per-layer complexity, sequential operations and dependency path lengths.
limitations: Reported applications are translation and parsing, not calibrated market forecasting.
The inspected HTML is a later author version; it should not be falsely described as a retrieved immutable 2017 page.
Attention weights are not automatically causal explanations or verified evidence.

title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
status: Peer-reviewed NAACL-HLT 2019, Volume 1, 4171-4186; distinguish from the earlier preprint
verification: ACL publisher metadata and abstract inspected.
supports: BERT pretrains deep bidirectional text representations and adapts them with task-specific output layers.
limitations: Language-task results are not market forecasting results.
A future-trained model or corpus can contaminate historical evaluations; this paper does not certify any model's as-of availability.

title: Domain-Adversarial Training of Neural Networks
status: Peer-reviewed; Journal of Machine Learning Research 17(59), 1-35
verification: Primary JMLR abstract, metadata and BibTeX inspected; both JMLR renderings shorten Marchand to March. The author-deposited arXiv:1505.07818 metadata explicitly gives Mario Marchand, the spelling used here.
supports: The paper learns task-discriminative but domain-indiscriminative representations from labeled source and unlabeled target data.
Its experiments include sentiment and image classification.
limitations: Does not guarantee successful transfer between market families or under arbitrary shift.
Unlabeled future data usage still needs an explicit evaluation protocol.

title: The Combination of Forecasts
status: Published journal article; Operational Research Quarterly 20(4), 451-468; modern publisher metadata uses the successor journal title Journal of the Operational Research Society
verification: Primary Taylor & Francis page citation metadata and complete publisher abstract in its ScholarlyArticle JSON-LD inspected. The simplified page omitted that abstract; no full article inspection is claimed. The issue metadata identifies 1969; a later online date is not the original publication date.
supports: The publisher abstract describes combining two sets of airline-passenger forecasts and finding that composite forecasts can have lower mean-square error than either original set.
It describes estimating combination weights from past forecast errors and comparing methods for doing so.
limitations: An empirical possibility is not a guarantee that every combination improves forecasts.
These point-forecast results are not a theorem that an average of event probabilities is calibrated.
Weight estimation and the historical availability of past errors still need a valid evaluation design.
locator: Publisher HTML head: ScholarlyArticle abstract; issue date metadata

title: Combining predictive distributions
status: Peer-reviewed; Electronic Journal of Statistics 7; inspected arXiv manuscript dates to 2011
verification: Author-deposited arXiv abstract inspected; published title, journal and year checked against publisher-deposited DOI metadata. Full version comparison not performed.
supports: The paper studies linear and nonlinear probability-distribution aggregation through coherence, calibration and dispersion.
The abstract identifies simulation and financial-return/weather case studies.
limitations: An average of forecasts is not automatically calibrated or coherent.
These case studies do not show prediction-market profitability.

title: Using Stacking to Average Bayesian Predictive Distributions (with Discussion)
status: Peer-reviewed; Bayesian Analysis 13(3); author manuscript posted in 2017
verification: Author-deposited abstract and related DOI inspected; journal title/year verified in publisher-deposited Crossref metadata. Discussion text not inspected.
supports: The paper extends stacking to predictive distributions and compares it with Bayesian model averaging in an M-open setting.
limitations: Its leave-one-out machinery is not automatically an appropriate validation split for time-dependent contracts.
Combination weights still require leakage-safe fitting and uncertainty assessment.

title: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting
status: Peer-reviewed; Journal of Computational Finance; institutional citation gives 2017
verification: Western Michigan University institutional citation, authors, DOI and abstract inspected. Full paper not inspected; 2017 publication not confused with earlier working-paper dates or 2016 in the DOI.
supports: The paper proposes a probability-of-backtest-overfitting framework and combinatorially symmetric cross-validation implementations for investment simulations.
limitations: The abstract's criticism of holdout in investment research does not license reuse of an untouched test set.
CSCV is not a universal cure for time dependence, shared event labels, or strategy selection.
locator: Institutional abstract and WMU ScholarWorks Citation

title: A Reality Check for Data Snooping
status: Peer-reviewed; Econometrica 68(5), 1097-1126
verification: University of Wisconsin-hosted original article inspected in memory: abstract/introduction opening (p. 1097) and Section 2a-2b through the stationary-bootstrap construction and beginning of Assumption C (pp. 1099-1104). Not all proofs, Appendix assumptions or empirical sections inspected.
supports: The Reality Check tests whether the best expected performance in a specified candidate family exceeds a benchmark, rather than testing only the selected winner in isolation.
The inspected setup uses stationary strong-mixing data, point-in-time predictors and asymptotic regularity conditions.
The bootstrap construction resamples dependent observations in common random-length blocks and centers candidate performance differences to construct a least-favorable-null comparison.
Accounting for other investigators' searched models requires their performance-difference records, not just their winning result.
limitations: The theory is asymptotic, not a finite-sample or arbitrary-dependence guarantee.
Candidate-family disclosure, justified dependence/block-length conditions and treatment of estimated parameters remain necessary.
The paper does not repair label leakage, unobserved strategy trials, incorrect fills or omitted costs; not all regularity proofs were inspected.
locator: Abstract p. 1097; Section 2a-2b, pp. 1099-1104; Propositions 2.1-2.2 and stationary-bootstrap construction

title: Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing
status: Peer-reviewed; Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 57(1), 289-300
verification: Publisher-deposited Crossref metadata and full deposited abstract inspected. Direct publisher response did not expose the article text.
supports: False discovery rate concerns the expected proportion of falsely rejected hypotheses.
The abstract states a control result for independent test statistics.
limitations: Do not assert arbitrary-dependence control for the original procedure.
Valid input p-values and a defined test family are still required.

title: The Stationary Bootstrap
status: Peer-reviewed; Journal of the American Statistical Association 89(428), 1303-1313
verification: Complete primary Taylor & Francis abstract inspected; author publication listing at https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~politis/DPpublication.html corroborates bibliographic identity. Original full article not inspected. WHITE2000 separately supplies an inspected exposition of the resampling construction.
supports: The stationary bootstrap resamples blocks with geometrically distributed random lengths for weakly dependent stationary observations.
The publisher abstract describes conditional stationarity of the resampled pseudo-series and develops consistency/weak-convergence properties.
limitations: Original full proofs and a particular block-length choice were not inspected.
The abstract does not guarantee confidence-interval validity for nonstationary or arbitrarily dependent event data.
A named bootstrap is not a substitute for specifying the sampling unit and relevant dependence.

title: Time-uniform, nonparametric, nonasymptotic confidence sequences
status: Peer-reviewed; The Annals of Statistics 49(2); inspected author HTML version arXiv:1810.08240v9 is later
verification: Author abstract and metadata inspected; publication year checked in DOI record. Relevant full HTML Section 2, Preliminaries: linear boundaries, including Definitions 1-2 and conditional-expectation setup, inspected at https://arxiv.org/html/1810.08240v9.
supports: Confidence sequences provide simultaneous-in-time coverage under specified process assumptions.
The inspected setup targets average conditional expectations and requires an appropriate filtration and exponential-supermartingale condition.
limitations: Time-uniformity is not assumption-free and does not fix a leaked dataset or a misspecified outcome target.
Repeated observations of one event cannot be treated as independent Bernoulli trials merely because monitoring is sequential.

title: A New Interpretation of Information Rate
status: Published journal article; Bell System Technical Journal 35(4), 917-926
verification: All ten pages of the Princeton-hosted article reproduction, pp. 917-926, inspected in memory. The copy states reproduced with permission of AT&T and identifies J. L. Kelly, Jr. as author. Bell Labs landing-page access remained unavailable; no PDF was saved or redistributed.
supports: The repeated-betting criterion maximizes expected log capital and differs from maximizing expected terminal capital.
The binary example shows why repeatedly staking all capital can lead to eventual ruin despite attractive expected capital.
The general model assumes independent transmitted symbols and noise; the track-take treatment explicitly permits holding capital unbet.
The conclusion limits its dominance comparison to fixed allocations for each received symbol and identifies reinvestment and control over stake sizes as essential requirements.
limitations: The original does not establish dominance over every time-varying adaptive strategy; it explicitly leaves further theorems open.
Known model probabilities, repeated opportunities and feasible reinvestment are not assured for an estimated event-market forecast.
Log-growth optimality does not guarantee finite-horizon safety or validate a universal fractional-Kelly rule, drawdown limit or affordable stake.
The paper uses base-two logarithms; changing log base rescales the growth objective without changing its optimizer.
locator: The gambler with a private wire, pp. 918-920; The general case, pp. 920-922; track take, pp. 923-925; Conclusion, pp. 925-926

title: Bid, ask and transaction prices in a specialist market with heterogeneously informed traders
status: Peer-reviewed; Journal of Financial Economics 14(1), 71-100
verification: Author-hosted Stanford/Columbia reprint visually inspected on PDF pp. 1-3: title, abstract and opening Section 1 discussion. The publication link was located on Paul Milgrom's Stanford publications page. Remaining formal model/proofs were not inspected.
supports: Superior information can generate a positive bid-ask spread even with a risk-neutral specialist and zero expected transaction profits.
The inspected introduction describes buy/sell direction as information used in the specialist's conditional valuation.
The model's zero-profit competitive pricing abstracts from transaction costs and binding inventory/cash constraints.
limitations: A specialist-stock-market model is an explicitly qualified analogy, not direct empirical evidence about any prediction venue.
The inspected text warns that binding inventory constraints can force departure from zero-profit pricing.
No detailed proposition beyond the inspected introduction or numerical event-market spread estimate is certified.
locator: Author-hosted reprint PDF pp. 1-3; abstract and opening Section 1

title: Continuous Auctions and Insider Trading
status: Peer-reviewed; Econometrica 53(6), 1315-1336
verification: Econometric Society primary citation and complete abstract inspected in the raw HTML abstract element; simplified fetching had previously omitted it. No full article inspection or login attempted.
supports: The dynamic sequential-auction model includes one risk-neutral insider, random noise traders and competitive risk-neutral market makers.
In the described continuous-trading equilibrium limit, the model has Brownian prices, constant depth and full eventual incorporation of the insider's information.
limitations: These are equilibrium conclusions under the specified model, not empirical laws of event-market prices.
Detailed proof conditions were not inspected beyond the primary abstract.
Do not infer informed counterparties, constant liquidity or full information aggregation in a particular contract from this source alone.

title: High-frequency trading in a limit order book
status: Peer-reviewed; Quantitative Finance 8(3), 217-224
verification: NYU author-hosted published article main text inspected in memory, Sections 1-3, pp. 217-223 (PDF pp. 1-7), including equations 1, 8, 12, 20, 29-30 and Section 3.3 numerical simulations. Appendix not fully inspected.
supports: The main model uses a driftless arithmetic-Brownian stock mid-price, constant volatility, exponential terminal-wealth utility and distance-dependent Poisson arrivals.
The frozen-inventory reservation price shifts down for a long inventory; it is a subjective valuation, not an executable midpoint fill.
The simple quoted reservation-price/spread expressions in equations 29-30 come from an approximation with symmetric exponential arrival rates, not a universally exact solution.
Reported performance comparisons are numerical simulations under specified parameters rather than historical executable returns.
limitations: The paper focuses on inventory risk, not a complete informed-order-flow or adverse-selection model.
Continuous costless quote updates, one-share fills and a terminal mid-price mark abstract from fees, queue priority, latency, cancellation and liquidation costs.
Unbounded Brownian stock prices and vanishing horizon inventory risk do not transfer unchanged to bounded event payouts with settlement jumps.
The general control problem and its simple approximate quote formula must not be conflated.

title: Efficient Market Making via Convex Optimization, and a Connection to Online Learning
status: Peer-reviewed; ACM Transactions on Economics and Computation 1(2), article 12, 1-39
verification: Microsoft Research author-institution metadata and full abstract inspected; title, author list, journal, volume, issue and DOI cross-checked against publisher-deposited metadata.
supports: The paper develops convex-cost market design over combinatorial or infinite outcome spaces with bounded-payoff securities.
Its abstract connects convex-hull optimization, bounded market-maker budgets and online learning.
limitations: Institutional mechanism design is not a guarantee that a trader can execute a mispriced basket.
Computational feasibility does not settle contract-rule equivalence or leg risk.

title: Doubly Robust Policy Evaluation and Learning
status: ICML 2011, as identified by the author-deposited manuscript; not the later expanded paper
verification: Author-deposited arXiv abstract, author list and ICML publication note inspected.
supports: Policy evaluation from contextual-bandit logs must address differences between logged and target action distributions.
The paper combines reward and past-policy models using doubly robust estimation.
limitations: The inspected abstract does not establish validity without action support, observed propensities, or suitable assumptions.
Historical passive market data are not automatically contextual-bandit logs for an execution policy.

title: Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning without Exploration
status: Peer-reviewed ICML proceedings; PMLR 97, 2052-2062
verification: Primary proceedings abstract and bibliographic export inspected.
supports: The paper demonstrates extrapolation problems when standard off-policy deep RL learns from fixed data unlike the current policy distribution.
It proposes batch-constrained action selection.
limitations: Continuous-control benchmark results do not validate market execution or simulator realism.
A constrained policy is not guaranteed safe or profitable in live markets.

title: Test In The Demo Environment
status: Mutable official documentation; year denotes inspected edition, not original publication
verification: Complete official page inspected after locating it through https://docs.kalshi.com/llms.txt.
supports: Kalshi provides a mock-funds demo with credentials separate from production.
The page explicitly warns that demo prices and behavior may not reflect real markets.
limitations: A demo is a mechanics test, not verified live-liquidity simulation or profitability evidence.
locator: Opening paragraphs, Warning and endpoint table

title: Historical Data
status: Mutable official documentation; inspected edition
verification: Official Overview, How It Works, Cutoff Timestamps, Historical Endpoints and beginning of Impacted Live Endpoints inspected.
supports: Live/historical partitions use moving cutoff timestamps available via GET /historical/cutoff.
Different object types use different partition times; events and series remain available through their original endpoints.
limitations: The inspected endpoint list does not establish a complete historical order-book archive.
Documentation is not a redistribution license or a verified history-coverage guarantee.

title: Orderbook Responses
status: Mutable official documentation; inspected fixed-point schema
verification: Official request format, response structure, bid arrays, reciprocal-relationship explanation and spread calculation inspected.
supports: The inspected schema returns orderbook_fp with yes_dollars/no_dollars bid arrays containing string dollar prices and fixed-point counts.
Under ordinary binary mechanics, opposite-outcome bids imply asks.
limitations: The schema and base root may change.
A displayed level is not a promised fill after latency, and a present book is not its history.
locator: Response Structure; Why Only Bids?; Calculating Spreads

title: Fee Rounding
status: Mutable official documentation; inspected edition
verification: Complete official page inspected, including precision, component definitions and per-order accumulator examples.
supports: The inspected guide distinguishes trade fee, rounding fee and rebate, with balance precision depending on membership/clearing type.
Rounding accumulation is maintained across fills of an order.
limitations: This is not the complete market-specific trade-fee schedule.
Do not replace it with a universal flat per-unit fee or imply hypothetical classroom fees are actual venue fees.

title: Fees
status: Mutable predictions-product documentation; not the separate U.S. product's fee schedule
verification: Official page inspected through Fee Precision, including fee formula and category table; discovered via https://docs.polymarket.com/llms.txt.
supports: The inspected guide describes market-specific taker fees depending on share price and quantity.
The guide distinguishes fee-free categories and maker treatment rather than assuming universal zero fees.
limitations: The category table is time-varying and should not be embedded as a timeless constant.
USDC fee descriptions and pUSD collateral documentation require explicit unit/product reconciliation; rebates are not guaranteed strategy profits.

title: Resolution
